title: The right to repair
text: When a farmer cannot repair his own tractor, or a city cannot fix its own buses, something has gone {{1}} with product design. That is the argument behind the growing 'right to repair' movement, which {{2}} manufacturers to make spare parts, tools and manuals available for years after a product is sold. The campaign gained ground when farmers began hacking software to keep ageing machinery {{3}}, and when videos of deliberately destroyed gadgets spread online. Opponents counter that safety and intellectual property justify restrictions, and that some repairs are genuinely {{4}} for amateurs. Regulators in several continents have taken a middle path, {{5}} repairability scores on everything from phones to lawnmowers. Consumers, it turns out, do look at the scores. Early data from France suggests products with better scores now {{6}} slightly higher prices and longer warranties. Design for repair also has an unexpected {{7}}: it creates local jobs, since repairs cannot be {{8}} abroad.

gaps.explanation: 'has gone wrong' — stopped working correctly; go does not combine with faulty, broken or mistaken.
'obliges manufacturers to make' — oblige + object + to; demand and hope take other patterns, and prevent takes 'from + -ing'.
'keep ageing machinery running' — keep + object + -ing; idle, parked and dismantled reverse the purpose.
'some repairs are genuinely dangerous for amateurs' — the opponents' safety argument needs the risk adjective; the others would not justify restrictions.
'requiring repairability scores' — making them compulsory; pin, hang and sketch describe drawing or attaching, not regulating.
'products with better scores now sell for slightly higher prices' — fetch; charge, pay and buy need a person or shop as the subject.
'an unexpected benefit' — a positive outcome; invoices, receipts and refunds are paperwork, not gains.
'repairs cannot be outsourced abroad' — sent to external contractors; imported and purchased mean bringing or buying in.
